units.title: Decolonization in Africa
units.intro: Why after 1945? Weakened Europe, UN talk of self-determination, wartime African service, educated nationalist elites, Cold War rivalry (both blocs court nationalists), mass parties and strikes.

f2.title: Colonial power shaped the exit. Portuguese and settler regimes fought longest.

lessons.title: Factors that led to independence in Africa

cards.title: 3.1 Factors that led to independence in Africa
body: For most African countries, the process was a peaceful one.
Independence came as a result of negotiations between the colonial power and representatives from the colony.

In contrast, in the colonies with large numbers of European settlers (such as Algeria, Kenya and Zimbabwe), the process involved lengthy wars of liberation before the colonial powers were forced to accept majority rule.
The world wars drained the economies of the European colonial powers.
The colonial powers also realized that they did not have to keep political power to maintain economic influence in their former colonies.

cards.title: Weighing the three factors (exam-style)
body: **A. Decline of the colonial powers.** The world wars left Europe too poor to hold its empires, and the powers realized they could keep economic influence without political rule. Criticism: this view is **Eurocentric**, as if Europeans alone decided.

**B. African nationalism.** After WWII united African movements forced the colonizers out. Criticism: in some places (such as French West Africa) independence came without a strong nationalist movement.
**C. The Cold War.** The USA and USSR both opposed old empires because they wanted influence in the new states.
**Conclusion.** Most historians say independence came from a **combination** of all three.
**Memory trick:** "Weak Europe, Strong Africa, Superpower pressure."

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2022)
cards.q: The French settlers in Algeria were known as **______**.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The term **'Colons'** (or *Pieds-Noirs*) refers to the European (mostly French) settlers who lived in Algeria during the period of French colonial rule. They held significant political and economic power until independence in 1962.

**Step 2:** So the answer is C) Colons.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Model answer: why Africa became independent
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the factors that led to independence in Africa after 1945.

steps.text: Weakened Europe: the world wars drained the economies of the European colonial powers.
Changed thinking: the powers realised they did not need political power to keep economic influence in their former colonies.
Path 1 – negotiation: for most African countries independence came peacefully through negotiations between the colonial power and representatives of the colony.
Path 2 – war: in settler colonies (Algeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe) lengthy wars of liberation were needed before majority rule was accepted.

cards.answer: Exhausted colonial economies and the belief that economic influence could continue without rule led to independence – mostly negotiated, but won by long wars where European settlers were numerous.

cards.title: 3.2 Decolonization in British Colonies
body: Ghana, and Nkrumah, became an inspiration to other nationalist movements in Africa.
A year before, in 1956, the Sudan gained its independence from the British.
Beginning from 1899 Sudan was formally under AngloEgyptian rule where it was run by a governor-general appointed by Egypt with British consent.
In reality, Sudan was effectively a British colony.
In 1954 Egypt gave up its claims to authority in the Sudan, a claim which dated back to the precolonial conquest of Mohammed Ali.

cards.title: Colonial power shaped the exit. Portuguese and settler regimes fought longest.
Decolonization in British Colonies
body:
- **British:** often staged constitutions. Model case: Gold Coast / Ghana under Nkrumah (1957), then a wave in the 1960s. Kenya includes Mau Mau; settler politics complicate it.
- **French:** at first “French Union / Community”; Guinea says no in 1958. Algeria: long, bitter war until 1962.
- **Belgian Congo:** sudden 1960 independence, almost no preparation, then crisis and foreign meddling.
- **Portuguese:** Lisbon treats colonies as provinces; armed struggle in Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau until the 1974 Lisbon coup.
- **Italian:** Libya earlier; Horn trusteeships (including the UN path that affected Eritrea — the book treats the national struggle in Unit 5).
- **Southern Africa:** apartheid South Africa, UDI Rhodesia, Portuguese neighbours — freedom delayed into the 1970s–90s (Zimbabwe 1980, Namibia 1990, democratic SA 1994).

cards.title: Model answer: how the British decolonised
cards.problem: (Short answer) Describe how Britain decolonised its African colonies, with examples.

steps.text: Method: Britain often staged constitutions – step-by-step transfer of power.
Model case: the Gold Coast became Ghana under Nkrumah in 1957 (Sudan in 1956 even earlier); then a wave of independence in the 1960s.
Complication: where there were white settlers (e.g. Kenya, Rhodesia) settler politics made it harder.
Southern Africa: freedom was delayed – Zimbabwe 1980, Namibia 1990, democratic South Africa 1994.

cards.answer: Britain mostly transferred power step by step through constitutions (Sudan 1956, Ghana 1957, then many in the 1960s), but settler colonies took longer.

cards.title: 3.3 Decolonization in French colonies
body: In 1958, France offered its colonies in French West Africa and French Equatorial Africa the choice of becoming independent countries within the French Community (with economic aid from France) or fully independent.
In the French Community, each state would run its own internal affairs, but would send representatives to a central council in Paris which would control foreign policy and defense.
Only Guinea chose full independence and cut all ties with France.
When Guinea opted for full independence instead of joining the French Community, France decided to teach it a lesson.
France tried to cripple the new state, by withdrawing all aid, personnel and equipment.

cards.title: Case study: the Algerian War of Independence (1954–1962)
body: **Step 1 – why France refused.** Algeria was France's main colony of white settlement, with about **two million French settlers (colons)** by 1945, so France was determined not to give independence.

**Step 2 – the awakening.** In **May 1945** colonial police fired on a peaceful nationalist demonstration at **Setif**. In the rioting and French reprisals, about a hundred Europeans and up to **8,000 Algerians** were killed.

**Step 3 – the war begins.** French reforms in 1946–47 were no longer enough. The **National Liberation Front (FLN)** launched the war in **November 1954**, starting from isolated rural areas. In August 1955 the uprising reached **Constantine**, and France began sending tens of thousands of troops.

**Step 4 – escalation.** By 1958 there were up to **half a million French troops** in Algeria. Each attempt at repression brought new recruits to the FLN, and hundreds of thousands of Algerians, mostly civilians, were killed.

**Step 5 – independence.** Despite internal divisions in the FLN, by 1962 France had to negotiate. Algeria became independent in **1962** after a war in which about 20,000 French and a million Algerians died. **Ahmed Ben Bella** of the FLN became the first president.

**Step 6 – why it matters.** Algeria was the **only French colony to fight a full-scale armed struggle before independence**, and the war pushed France to grant independence to its other African colonies.
**Memory trick:** "Setif 45 sparked it, FLN 54 fought it, Ben Bella 62 won it."

cards.title: Guinea 1958: the one colony that said "No" to France
body: **Step 1 – de Gaulle's offer.** In 1958 France offered its African colonies membership of the **French Community**: each would run its own internal affairs but send representatives to a council in Paris that controlled foreign policy and defence.
**Step 2 – Guinea's choice.** Only **Guinea** chose full independence and cut all ties with France.

**Step 3 – France's punishment.** France withdrew all aid, personnel and equipment – even telephones and light bulbs – destroyed files and dismissed Guinean soldiers without pensions. When the new president, **Sékou Touré**, moved into the former governor's house, everything had been smashed.
**Step 4 – who helped.** The **Soviet Union** stepped in with aid.

**Step 5 – the domino effect.** The other colonies soon wanted the same independence as British West Africa, and by the end of **1960** France agreed to full independence for its colonies in West and Equatorial Africa and Madagascar.
**Memory trick:** "Guinea said No in 58; everyone else got Yes in 60."

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2024)
cards.q: A French colony in Africa that chose complete independence rather than joining French to the community in 1958 was:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “When Guinea opted for full independence instead of joining the French Community, France decided to teach it a lesson.”

**Step 2:** **Step 1:** Recall the 1958 French Constitutional Referendum proposed by Charles de Gaulle.
**Step 2:** French colonies were given a choice: join the 'French Community' (limited autonomy) or take immediate independence (cutting all ties with France).
**Step 3:** **Guinea**, led by Ahmed Sékou Touré, was the only colony to vote 'No' to the community and choose immediate independence.
**Result:** Guinea.

**Step 3:** So the answer is B) Guinea.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Model answer: the French Community
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the French Community of 1958 and the case of Guinea.

steps.text: The offer (1958): French West and Equatorial African colonies could be independent within the French Community (with French economic aid) or fully independent.
How the Community worked: each state ran its internal affairs but sent representatives to a council in Paris that controlled foreign policy and defence.
Guinea: the only colony to choose full independence and cut all ties with France.
France's reaction: it withdrew all aid, personnel and equipment to cripple the new state.

cards.answer: The Community offered self-rule under Paris's control of foreign policy and defence; only Guinea chose full independence and was punished by France's withdrawal of all aid.

cards.title: 3.4 Decolonization in Belgian colonies
body: The transfer of power took place more suddenly in the Belgian Congo than anywhere else.
Initially Belgium wanted a 30-year period to prepare her colony for independence.
In the other Belgian colonies - Rwanda and Burundi - the legacy of Belgian rule resulted in civil war and genocide.
In both territories, the Belgians had used the minority Tutsi in the administration to control the majority Hutu.
After independence, deep-seated ill-feelings between the two groups got worse.

cards.title: The Belgian legacy in Rwanda and Burundi
body: **Step 1 – divide and rule.** In Rwanda and Burundi the Belgians governed through the **minority Tutsi**, using them in the administration to control the **majority Hutu**.
**Step 2 – after independence.** The resentment between the two groups grew worse once the Belgians left, leading to civil war.
**Step 3 – genocide.** In **1994** ethnic tension in **Rwanda** grew into full-scale genocide: extremist Hutus killed Tutsis and moderate Hutus, and almost **one million people** died.

**Step 4 – compare the Congo.** In the Belgian Congo, Belgium first planned a 30-year transition but suddenly granted independence in **June 1960** after violent protests; the army mutinied and civil war broke out.
**Memory trick:** "Belgium ruled the many through the few – Rwanda paid in 1994."
**Exam tip:** The Hutu–Tutsi conflict is described as the colonial legacy of Belgium.

cards.problem: (Short answer) Why did Belgian decolonisation lead to crisis and conflict?

steps.text: Congo: the transfer of power was the most sudden anywhere – Belgium had wanted 30 years, but independence came in 1960 with almost no preparation.
Result in Congo: crisis and foreign meddling right after independence.
Rwanda and Burundi: Belgium had ruled through the minority Tutsi over the majority Hutu.
Result: deep ill-feeling grew worse after independence, leading to civil war and genocide.

cards.answer: Sudden independence without preparation (Congo 1960) and divide-and-rule between Tutsi and Hutu (Rwanda, Burundi) left crisis, civil war and genocide.

cards.title: 3.5 Decolonization in Portuguese colonies
body: By the 1970s these wars were costing almost half the Portuguese budget and involving increasing numbers of troops.
In 1974, army officers in Portugal, who were determined to end the futile colonial wars, overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal.
The new government quickly granted independence to the three colonies.
Mozambique, Samora Machel, the leader of FRELIMO (Front for the Liberation of Mozambique), became the first president.

The situation in Angola was complicated by the existence of three rival resistance groups, superpower backing the two rival groups, and the involvement of Apartheid South Africa and Cuba (See next unit).

cards.title: Guinea-Bissau: the case study in steps
body: **1956** – Amilcar Cabral founds the **PAIGC**. **1959** – the Bissau dockworkers' strike is crushed and fifty workers are killed; this turning point leads to armed struggle. **1963** – the liberation war begins; liberated rural areas get schools, clinics, roads and farming projects. **September 1973** – the PAIGC declares an independent state. **January 1974** – Cabral is assassinated. **April 1974** – Portuguese officers, including General Spinola, who had commanded in Guinea and saw the war could not be won, overthrow the dictatorship. **September 1974** – Portuguese troops leave; all Portuguese colonies are independent by **1975**.
**Key point.** The African liberation wars themselves caused the coup in Portugal.
**Memory trick:** "56 party, 59 massacre, 63 war, 73 state, 74 coup."

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2014)
cards.q: The following were Portuguese colonies in Africa **except**:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Egypt was never a Portuguese colony. It was part of the Ottoman Empire and later came under British influence/protection. Mozambique, Angola, and Guinea-Bissau were all major Portuguese colonies in Africa.

**Step 2:** So the answer is D) Egypt.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

**Step 2:** Identify the colonial history of Rwanda. Rwanda was initially part of German East Africa and later became a Belgian mandate/trust territory after WWI.
**Result:** Rwanda was not a Portuguese colony.

**Step 2:** So the answer is D) Rwanda.

cards.title: Model answer: Portuguese decolonisation
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did Portugal's African colonies win independence only in the mid-1970s?

steps.text: Portugal's view: Lisbon treated its colonies as provinces and refused to leave.
Armed struggle: wars of liberation in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.
The cost: by the 1970s these wars took almost half the Portuguese budget and ever more troops.

Turning point: in 1974 army officers overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal and granted independence; FRELIMO's Samora Machel became Mozambique's first president, while Angola's three rival movements, superpowers, South Africa and Cuba complicated its independence.

cards.answer: Portugal held on until armed struggle made the wars unbearably costly; the 1974 Lisbon coup then brought quick independence to Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.

cards.title: 3.6 Decolonization in Italian colonies
body: Italy lost all its African Colonies in the course of the Second World War.
The majority of Eritreans favored complete independence, but their ambitions were frustrated by the intervention of Ethiopia.
Ethiopia saw the period of decolonization as an ideal opportunity to gain an outlet to the sea.
At the United Nations, powerful states especially the USA favored Ethiopian claims.
The UN therefore denied Eritreans their right to self-determination and, preferring to hand Eritrea to Ethiopia in 1952 by way of an unviable federation.

cards.title: Eritrea: decolonization denied, armed struggle from 1961
body: **Step 1 – British rule.** After Italy's defeat in the Second World War, Eritrea came under **British occupation in 1941**.

**Step 2 – independence denied.** Most Eritreans wanted full independence, but Ethiopia wanted an outlet to the sea, and powerful states, especially the USA, supported Ethiopia's claim at the UN. The UN denied Eritrea self-determination and joined it to Ethiopia in **1952** through an unworkable **federation**.
**Step 3 – annexation.** Emperor **Haile Selassie** abolished the federation and annexed Eritrea as Ethiopia's fourteenth province in **1962**.

**Step 4 – armed struggle.** The **ELF** began the armed struggle on **1 September 1961**, when **Hamid Idris Awate** fired the first shot against Ethiopian forces near **Mount Adal**. It took thirty years (until 1991) to win independence.
**Memory trick:** "41 British, 52 federated, 61 first shot, 62 annexed, 91 free."
**Exam tip:** The start of the Eritrean armed struggle is 1961 (Awate, Mount Adal) – a year before the annexation of 1962.

cards.title: Model answer: Eritrea and decolonisation
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain why Eritrea did not become independent when Italian colonialism ended.

steps.text: Italy lost all its African colonies during the Second World War.
The Eritrean majority favoured complete independence.
Ethiopia intervened: it saw decolonisation as the ideal chance to gain an outlet to the sea.
At the UN powerful states, especially the USA, favoured Ethiopia's claims, so the UN denied self-determination and federated Eritrea with Ethiopia in 1952 – an unviable federation.

cards.answer: Ethiopia's wish for a sea outlet, backed by the USA at the UN, led to the 1952 federation that denied Eritreans the independence most of them wanted.

lessons.title: The struggle for freedom in South and Southern Africa

cards.title: 3.7 The struggle for freedom in South and Southern Africa
body: Not surprisingly, in South Africa, the country with the largest population of white settlers, resistance to African majority rule had been strong.
South Africa, was not, strictly speaking, a colony in the same sense as the other colonies of Africa.
African majority rule in South Africa would have to be achieved through the struggles of the majority of South Africans.
In 1948 a National Party, a party of Afrikaner supremacist won an overall majority in the whites-only general election.
The National Party Government reinforced the segregationist system developed over the previous fifty years.

cards.title: Liberation movements and Black Consciousness in Southern Africa
body: **Step 1 – match each movement to its country.** **SWAPO** – Namibia; **ZANU** (and ZAPU) – Zimbabwe; **FRELIMO** – Mozambique; **MPLA** – Angola; **PAIGC** (founded 1956 by **Amílcar Cabral**) – Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde.

**Step 2 – Namibia.** A former German colony, it was given to South Africa as a mandate in 1920. After 1948 South Africa applied apartheid there and refused to hand it to the UN. The UN recognized SWAPO as the true representative, and after SWAPO's guerrilla war (helped by Cuban forces) and Western pressure, Namibia became independent in **1990**.

**Step 3 – Black Consciousness.** In the early 1970s black workers' strikes spread, and among black students a new Africanist movement, **Black Consciousness**, led by **Steve Biko**, aimed to restore black self-respect and win liberation without relying on white liberals.

**Step 4 – Soweto.** On **16 June 1976** police fired on 15,000 schoolchildren protesting in **Soweto**. Revolt spread across the country, at least 600 people died in 1976–77, and Biko was beaten to death in police custody (1977).
**Step 5 – the ANC story.** ANC founded **1912**; the PAC broke away from it; **Nelson Mandela** became the first black president (1994), followed by **Thabo Mbeki** (1999).
**Memory trick:** "Biko – Black Consciousness; Mbeki – Mandela's successor."

cards.title: Model answer: why South Africa's freedom came late
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did majority rule come to South Africa so much later than to most of Africa?

steps.text: Largest white settler population in Africa, so resistance to African majority rule was strong.
Not strictly a colony: majority rule had to be won by the struggles of the majority of South Africans themselves.
1948: the Afrikaner-supremacist National Party won the whites-only election and reinforced segregation (apartheid).
Long struggle: ANC leader Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison and became the first black president in the democratic elections of 1994.

cards.answer: A large, powerful settler minority and the apartheid state of the National Party (from 1948) blocked majority rule until the long struggle succeeded in 1994.

cards.title: 3.8 Organization of African Unity
body: In the early 1960s, as more African states became independent, there was growing support for African unity, which was one of the ideals of Pan-Africanism (see grade 11 textbook).
The Casablanca bloc, led by Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, wanted a federation of all African countries.
The group included Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali and Libya.
The Monrovian bloc, led by Senghor of Senegal, felt that unity should be achieved gradually, through economic cooperation.
The differences of opinion were resolved when the emperor of Ethiopia, Haile Selassie, invited both groups to a meeting in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia.

cards.title: Background: what Pan-Africanism was (Grade 11 recap)
body: **Step 1 – the idea.** Pan-Africanism was the idea of uniting all black Africans, whatever their national boundaries, in a common struggle for dignity, freedom and self-rule.
**Step 2 – where it began.** It started among people of African descent in the United States and the Caribbean. Its two best-known leaders were **W.E.B. Du Bois** and **Marcus Garvey**.
**Step 3 – the cultural side.** At the same time the **Negritude** movement (associated with Léopold Senghor) stressed the uniqueness and value of African culture and history.

**Step 4 – into Africa.** Between the wars, a new generation of African leaders educated in Europe and the USA – Jomo Kenyatta (Kenya), Léopold Senghor (Senegal), Nnamdi Azikiwe (Nigeria) and later Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana) – took these ideas home and used them to demand independence.

**Step 5 – the link to the OAU.** Once many states were independent in the early 1960s, the Pan-African dream of unity became a practical question: a full federation at once (Casablanca bloc) or gradual cooperation (Monrovia bloc). The compromise was the OAU, founded in Addis Ababa in 1963.
**Memory trick:** "Du Bois and Garvey dreamed it, Nkrumah pushed it, the OAU built it."

cards.title: Organization of African Unity
body: **OAU (1963, Addis Ababa):** African unity, respect for inherited borders (to avoid border wars), support for remaining liberation movements. Ancestor of today’s AU.

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2020)
cards.q: Which of the following countries was a member of the Monrovian group?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The differences of opinion were resolved when the emperor of Ethiopia, Haile Selassie, invited both groups to a meeting in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia.”

**Step 2:** Before the OAU was formed, African leaders were divided into two groups: The **Monrovia Group** (moderate, including **Ethiopia**, Nigeria, and Liberia) and the Casablanca Group (radical, including Ghana, Egypt, and Mali).

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) Ethiopia.

cards.q: Recognized African leader proposed **Regional Union** of African states economically and politically in 1960s was ...
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The Casablanca bloc, led by Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, wanted a federation of all African countries.”

**Step 2:** Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana was the most vocal advocate for the immediate political and economic unification of Africa (the 'United States of Africa'). He believed that individual African states were too weak to survive alone against neo-colonialism.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) Kwame Nkrumah.

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2017)
cards.q: Which of the following countries **was not** allowed to join the OAU in 1963?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “OAU (1963, Addis Ababa): African unity, respect for inherited borders, support for remaining liberation movements (apartheid South Africa was excluded).”

**Step 2:** South Africa was not allowed to join the OAU in 1963 because of its institutionalized system of racial segregation known as **Apartheid**. The OAU's primary goal was to end colonialism and white minority rule in Africa.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) South Africa.

cards.title: Model answer: founding of the OAU
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how the OAU was formed in 1963 and what its aims were.

steps.text: Background: as more states became independent in the early 1960s, support grew for African unity, an ideal of Pan-Africanism.

Two blocs: the Casablanca bloc (Nkrumah of Ghana; Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali, Libya) wanted a federation of all Africa; the Monrovian bloc (Senghor of Senegal) wanted gradual unity through economic cooperation.
Compromise: Emperor Haile Selassie invited both groups to Addis Ababa, and the OAU was founded there in 1963.
Aims: African unity, respect for inherited borders (to avoid border wars) and support for remaining liberation movements.

cards.answer: The OAU (Addis Ababa, 1963) was a compromise between the Casablanca and Monrovian blocs, aiming at unity, respect for colonial borders and support for liberation movements.

tips.text: Decolonization in Africa in the 1960s and 1970s was mainly a result of nationalist movements that emerged in most African countries after the Second World War.
Other factors that contributed for African independence include: the weakening of colonial powers after the WWII and Cold War politics.
The British and French granted independence to their colonies in the 1950s and 1960s, mainly peacefully.
Problems arose where there were settlers of European descent, and there were major conflicts in areas such as Kenya, Algeria and Zimbabwe.
Belgium, though reluctant at first, also granted independence to its colonies in the 1960s.
The Portuguese were less willing to give up their colonies, and long wars of liberation took place in Angola and Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique, which lasted until the mid1970s.
One of the major post-independence developments in Africa was the creation of the Organization of African Unity (OAU) in 1963.
The Organization of African Unity was made up of all independent states that supported the charter.
In 2002, the OAU was replaced by the African Union.

questions.q: The first West African state to achieve its independence from colonial rule after the Second World War was ...
questions.label: 9. The first West African state to achieve its independence from colonial rule after the Second World…
why: Answer D: Ghana
From the lesson: “Italy lost all its African Colonies in the course of the Second World War.”
Ghana (formerly the Gold Coast) became the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from British colonial rule on March 6, 1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
So the answer is D) Ghana.

questions.q: One of the following is **correct** about the objectives of the Organization of African Unity (OAU).
questions.label: 10. One of the following is **correct** about the objectives of the Organization of African Unity (OAU).

options.A: To protect European colonialism in Africa
options.B: To cultivate totalitarian regimes in Africa
options.C: To raise the living standards of all Africans
options.D: To keep the racial laws of the Apartheid
options.E: To oppose institutionalization of human rights in Africa

why: Answer C: To raise the living standards of all Africans
From the lesson: “OAU (1963, Addis Ababa):   African unity, respect for inherited borders (to avoid border wars), support for remaining liberation movements.”
The OAU, founded in 1963, aimed to promote unity, coordinate cooperation for a better life for African peoples, and defend the sovereignty and independence of African states.
So the answer is C) To raise the living standards of all Africans.

why: Answer A: Kwame Nkrumah______TANU
From the lesson: “The Casablanca bloc, led by Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, wanted a federation of all African countries.”
**Kwame Nkrumah** led the **Convention People's Party (CPP)** in Ghana. **TANU** (Tanganyika African National Union) was led by **Julius Nyerere** in Tanzania.
So the answer is A) Kwame Nkrumah______TANU.

questions.q: Which statement is **wrong** about OAU?
questions.label: 13. Which statement is **wrong** about OAU?

options.A: Morocco is **not** a member of the organization
options.B: Changed its name from OAU to AU in 2002.
options.C: Its first secretary general was Sir Eric Drummond.
options.D: Its head office is in Addis Ababa

why: Answer C: Its first secretary general was Sir Eric Drummond.

**Sir Eric Drummond** was the first Secretary-General of the **League of Nations**, not the OAU. The first Secretary-General of the OAU was Diallo Telli of Guinea. Note: Morocco withdrew in 1984 but rejoined the AU in 2017.
So the answer is C) Its first secretary general was Sir Eric Drummond..
